evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with bipolar disorder: recognition and referral, specialist assessment, risk planning, mania, bipolar depression, long-term treatment, lithium, antipsychotic, valproate and lamotrigine monitoring, physical health. Verified against NICE CG185 and FDA labels; no Saudi guideline found; SFDA not checked.
findings: NICE CG185 recommendations for adults (sections 1.1 to 1.10) were read in full on 13 Oct 2026; sections for children and young people were not used. Doses and contraindications were read from US FDA labels via openFDA on the same date.
CG185 is a UK guideline; its MHRA valproate rules and the care programme approach do not apply directly in Saudi Arabia.
unverifiedSections: SFDA registration of lithium, quetiapine, lamotrigine and other agents not checked (the SFDA site refused automated access from the authoring environment)
No Saudi bipolar disorder guideline was found; none is cited
ICD or DSM diagnostic criteria are not reproduced
Doses for valproate, olanzapine, fluoxetine, haloperidol, risperidone, aripiprazole and asenapine are not given because no label was read for them
Valproate pregnancy-prevention requirements are UK MHRA rules; Saudi requirements were not checked
Pathophysiology beyond the points in CG185 is not covered because the recommendations do not describe it
Pregnancy, postnatal and perinatal management is in a separate NICE guideline and is not covered

pathophysiology.summary: Bipolar disorder is a long-term relapsing and remitting condition with episodes of mania or hypomania and bipolar depression, with symptoms that may persist between episodes. NICE CG185 applies to bipolar I, bipolar II, mixed affective and rapid cycling disorders. This topic covers adults only; the guideline's separate sections for children and young people are not used.
keyMechanisms: Bipolar disorder is commonly a long-term relapsing and remitting condition needing self-management and engagement with primary and secondary care and carers (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.7.1).

Mania and hypomania can lead to education, financial and employment problems and to risks such as excessive spending, exploitation and disinhibited or sexualised behaviour (NICE CG185 Recs 1.1.4 and 1.3.5).
Rapid cycling bipolar disorder is treated like other types because there is no strong evidence to treat it differently (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.1.3).
Triggers for episodes, early warning signs and patterns of relapse are part of the assessment and the risk management plan (NICE CG185 Recs 1.3.2 and 1.4.1).
An antidepressant taken alone may be associated with mania or hypomania; if that occurs NICE advises considering stopping it (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.2).

references.title: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 24 September 2014, last updated 2 September 2025, Recommendations 1.1.3–1.1.4, 1.3.2, 1.3.5, 1.4.1, 1.5.2 and 1.7.1

symptoms: Previous periods of overactivity or disinhibited behaviour; lasting 4 days or more should prompt specialist referral when someone presents with depression (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.1).
Mania or hypomania: overactivity, disinhibition and episodic, sustained changes in behaviour (NICE CG185 Recs 1.2.1 and 1.3.2).
Mixed affective state with both manic and depressive symptoms (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.11).
physicalSigns: CG185 lists no examination signs; assessment includes physical health, weight gain from medication and mental state (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.3.2).
Physical health checks cover weight or BMI, pulse, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids and liver function (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.12).
redFlags: Suspected mania, severe depression, or danger to self or others: refer urgently for specialist mental health assessment (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.2).
Immediate risk to self or others: follow the NICE violence and aggression and self-harm guidelines (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.4.2).
A woman with bipolar disorder who is pregnant or planning pregnancy: re-refer to secondary care if managed in primary care (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.9).
Lithium toxicity or neurotoxicity: paraesthesia, ataxia, tremor and cognitive impairment, which can occur at therapeutic levels (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.24).
Rash during lamotrigine dose increase: contact a doctor immediately (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.37).
precipitants: Alcohol, tobacco, prescribed and non-prescribed medicines and illicit drugs, which can interfere with treatment (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.2).
Personal, social, occupational or environmental triggers (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.4.1).
Poor adherence or rapid discontinuation of lithium raises relapse risk (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.14).

references.title: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 24 September 2014, last updated 2 September 2025, Recommendations 1.3.3 and 1.10.2

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and refer
actions: When an adult presents with depression, ask about previous overactivity or disinhibited behaviour; if it lasted 4 days or more, consider specialist assessment (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.1).
Refer urgently if mania or severe depression is suspected or the person is a danger to self or others (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.2).
Do not use questionnaires in primary care to identify bipolar disorder in adults (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.3).
Do not start lithium in primary care in someone who has not taken it before except under shared care, and do not start valproate in primary care (NICE CG185 Recs 1.2.7–1.2.8).

clinicalManagement.title: Specialist assessment, care plan and risk plan
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible after assessment
actions: Carry out a full psychiatric assessment and consider differential diagnoses (NICE CG185 Recs 1.3.2–1.3.3).

Develop a care plan with the person, give copies to the person and GP, and a risk management plan covering triggers, early warning signs, an agreed protocol for increasing medication, primary and secondary care agreements and crisis contacts (NICE CG185 Recs 1.3.4 and 1.4.1).
Offer crisis services when the person is in crisis (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.4.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Mania or hypomania
actions: Provide a calming environment with reduced stimulation; advise against important decisions until recovered (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.1).

Consider stopping an antidepressant taken as monotherapy, and offer an antipsychotic whether or not it is stopped; also consider stopping an antidepressant taken with a mood stabiliser (NICE CG185 Recs 1.5.2 and 1.5.7).
Do not offer lamotrigine, gabapentin or topiramate to treat mania (NICE CG185 Recs 1.5.12 and 1.10.4).

branches.condition: Not taking an antipsychotic or mood stabiliser
actions: Offer haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone according to preference and clinical context (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.3).

If poorly tolerated or ineffective at the maximum licensed dose, offer another from that list; if still insufficient, consider adding lithium, then valproate instead if lithium is ineffective or unsuitable, following the MHRA valproate safety measures (NICE CG185 Recs 1.5.4–1.5.6).
Check the plasma level and consider adding haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.8).

branches.condition: Already taking a mood stabiliser for prophylaxis
actions: Consider increasing the dose up to the BNF maximum, then adding haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.9).
Review adherence; consider increasing the dose if tolerated or changing treatment (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.10).

branches.condition: Severe or life-threatening mania not responding to other treatment
actions: ECT is an option under NICE technology appraisal guidance TA59 (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.13).
Treat as mania and monitor closely for depression (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Bipolar depression
actions: Offer a psychological intervention developed for bipolar disorder, or CBT, interpersonal therapy or behavioural couples therapy; monitor mood for mania or hypomania (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.6.1).
Take overdose toxicity into account in periods of high suicide risk and consider limiting supply (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.6.10).

branches.condition: Moderate or severe depression, not on treatment
actions: Offer fluoxetine with olanzapine, or quetiapine alone; if preferred consider olanzapine alone or lamotrigine alone; if no response to fluoxetine with olanzapine or quetiapine, consider lamotrigine alone (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.6.3).
Check the plasma level and raise the dose if inadequate; if at maximum, add fluoxetine with olanzapine or quetiapine; or if preferred olanzapine alone or lamotrigine (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.6.4).
Review adherence and consider a higher dose if tolerated; if limited response at the top of the range, add fluoxetine with olanzapine or quetiapine (NICE CG185 Recs 1.6.5–1.6.6).

clinicalManagement.title: Long-term treatment and physical health
actions: Within 4 weeks of resolution, discuss continuing treatment or starting long-term treatment; if continuing, a further 3 to 6 months then review (NICE CG185 Recs 1.5.14–1.5.15 and 1.6.11–1.6.12).

Offer lithium as first-line long-term drug treatment; if ineffective, poorly tolerated or unsuitable consider an antipsychotic such as asenapine, aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone, then valproate combined with an antipsychotic or lithium (NICE CG185 Recs 1.7.7–1.7.10).
Offer a structured psychological intervention designed for bipolar disorder to prevent relapse, and a family intervention where relevant (NICE CG185 Recs 1.7.2–1.7.4).

To stop treatment, reduce gradually, over at least 4 weeks (preferably up to 3 months for lithium) and monitor for relapse, continuing for 2 years after complete stopping (NICE CG185 Recs 1.7.11–1.7.12, 1.10.25 and 1.10.35).
Monitor physical health at least annually and offer a healthy eating and physical activity programme (NICE CG185 Recs 1.2.11–1.2.12 and 1.8.2).
Offer return to primary care with an agreed care plan once stable (NICE CG185 Recs 1.9.3–1.9.4).

regimens.indication: Long-term prevention in bipolar I disorder; add-on for mania
regimens.dose: FDA label: start 300 mg three times daily and raise by 300 mg every 3 days to the target level; usual dose for maintenance 300 to 600 mg two to three times daily (Table 1)
regimens.duration: Long term; stop gradually over at least 4 weeks, preferably up to 3 months (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.25)
adjustments: Plasma level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L when first prescribed; consider 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L for at least 6 months after relapse on lithium or subthreshold symptoms (NICE CG185 Recs 1.10.15–1.10.16)
FDA label: acute mania 0.8 to 1.2 mEq/L, maintenance 0.8 to 1.0 mEq/L; avoid in creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min (sections 2.2 and 2.5)
Older people: lower doses and watch interactions (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.3)
monitoring: Level 12 hours post dose at 1 week and after each dose change, weekly until stable, every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months or every 3 months in higher-risk groups (NICE CG185 Recs 1.10.15 and 1.10.19–1.10.20)
Weight or BMI, urea and electrolytes with calcium, eGFR and thyroid function every 6 months (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.21)
Check at every appointment for neurotoxicity: paraesthesia, ataxia, tremor and cognitive impairment (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.24)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to an inactive ingredient (FDA label section 4)
Boxed warning: lithium toxicity can occur at doses close to therapeutic concentrations
Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs; if prescribed, give regularly and monitor monthly then every 3 months (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.18)

adjustments: Elderly: lower starting dose (50 mg/day), slower titration; hepatic impairment: start 25 mg/day (FDA label sections 2.3–2.4)
Do not routinely exceed the maximum licensed dose (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.7)
monitoring: Pulse and blood pressure after each dose change; weight or BMI weekly for 6 weeks then at 12 weeks; fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.8)

regimens.indication: Bipolar depression (lamotrigine alone or added to lithium or valproate)
regimens.dose: Target 200 mg/day (100 mg/day with valproate; 400 mg/day with carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital or primidone and no valproate); slow titration: not taking valproate nor enzyme inducers, 25 mg daily for weeks 1 and 2, 50 mg daily for weeks 3 and 4, 100 mg daily in week 5, 200 mg in week 6 (FDA label Table 5)

regimens.duration: Maintenance reassessed periodically after 16 weeks (FDA label section 2.4); stopping: reduce over at least 4 weeks (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.39)
adjustments: Valproate users start 25 mg every other day for weeks 1 and 2, 25 mg daily weeks 3 and 4, 50 mg week 5, 100 mg weeks 6 and 7 (FDA label Table 5)
The recommended initial dose and escalation must not be exceeded because of rash risk (FDA label section 2.1)
monitoring: Advise the person to contact a doctor immediately for a rash during dose escalation (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.37)
Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests at start (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.36)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to the drug or its ingredients (FDA label section 4)
Do not use to treat mania (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.12)

medicationPlan.note: Valproate, olanzapine with fluoxetine, haloperidol, risperidone, aripiprazole and asenapine are recommended in CG185 but have no dose given here because no label was read for them. Valproate carries MHRA/UK pregnancy-prevention rules in CG185; check SFDA requirements, registration and the hospital formulary.

learningObjectives: Ask about past overactivity in anyone presenting with depression and refer correctly.
Choose acute treatment for mania and bipolar depression and plan long-term prevention.
Start and monitor lithium, antipsychotics, valproate and lamotrigine safely.
keyPoints: Do not use questionnaires in primary care to identify bipolar disorder.
Mania: antipsychotic first (haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone); consider stopping antidepressant monotherapy.
Bipolar depression: fluoxetine with olanzapine, or quetiapine alone; lamotrigine is an option.
Lithium is the first-line long-term drug; levels and renal, thyroid and calcium tests are scheduled.
Physical health is checked at least annually; monitoring continues for 2 years after stopping medication.
pitfalls: Starting lithium or valproate in primary care outside a shared-care arrangement (NICE CG185 Recs 1.2.7–1.2.8).
Using lamotrigine, gabapentin or topiramate for mania or bipolar disorder where CG185 advises against it (NICE CG185 Recs 1.5.12 and 1.10.4).
Stopping lithium or an antipsychotic abruptly (NICE CG185 Recs 1.10.13 and 1.10.25).
Prescribing over-the-counter NSAIDs to someone on lithium (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.18).
Continuing valproate in women and girls who can become pregnant without following the MHRA measures (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.27).
Forgetting regular physical health monitoring (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.8.4).

references.title: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 24 September 2014, last updated 2 September 2025

patientEducation: Explain that bipolar disorder is a long-term relapsing and remitting condition, with the benefits and risks of long-term treatment and the risk of relapse after stopping (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.7.1).
Give written information about purpose, side effects and monitoring of each medicine (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.1).

Lithium: seek medical help for diarrhoea, vomiting or acute illness; keep fluid intake up; tell the doctor if pregnant or planning pregnancy; avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs (NICE CG185 Recs 1.10.17–1.10.18).
Lamotrigine: contact a doctor immediately for a rash during dose increases (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.37).
Explain how alcohol, tobacco, other medicines and drugs can interfere with treatment (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.2).
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer a combined healthy eating and physical activity programme, especially for those on antipsychotics or long-term medication (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.8.2).
Identify and manage hypertension, abnormal lipids, obesity, diabetes risk and inactivity early (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.13).
Calming environments and reduced stimulation during mania or hypomania (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.5.1).
mdtReferrals: Specialist bipolar service, early intervention in psychosis service or specialist integrated community team (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.3.1).
Psychological therapists trained in bipolar disorder (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.6.2).
Carer education and support programme and family intervention (NICE CG185 Recs 1.1.8 and 1.7.2).
Reproductive and perinatal mental health services for pregnancy or planned pregnancy (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.2.9).
dischargeCriteria: Symptoms have responded and remain stable, the person wishes to return to primary care, and a care plan, crisis plan and medication review date are agreed (NICE CG185 Recs 1.9.3–1.9.4).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Primary care reviews treatment and care at least annually, and physical health at least annually (NICE CG185 Recs 1.2.4 and 1.2.11). Secondary care monitors antipsychotics for at least 12 months or until stable (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.10.9). Monitor symptoms, mood and mental state for 2 years after medication stops (NICE CG185 Rec. 1.7.12).
